stats_inference_one_sample.description: Estimate variance, select the correct t reference and test a normal population mean when its variance is unknown.

sections.title: Which denominator gives an unbiased variance?
sections.label: Estimate variability
sections.intro: Variation of individual records and variation of a sample mean describe different quantities.

blocks.html: Use \(s^2=\frac{\sum(x-\bar x)^2}{n-1}\) and \(\mathrm{SE}=\frac{s}{\sqrt n}\).
Do not divide the centred sum of squares by n when an unbiased variance is required.

blocks.title: Recover the sample mean, variance and estimated standard error
blocks.prompt:
The observations are \(9,\quad 11,\quad 12,\quad 12,\quad 16\).

Find the original mean, unbiased sample variance and estimated standard error of the mean. Give exact values.

retry.feedback: That uses a divisor of n. The unbiased sample variance divides the centred squares by n−1.

blocks.hint: The estimated standard error comes from the unbiased variance, not the raw sum of squares.
blocks.solution:
The sum is \(60\) and the sum of squares is \(746\). The sample has \(5\) observations.

After undoing any coding, the mean is \(12\). The unbiased variance is \(\frac{746-\frac{\left(60\right)^2}{5}}{4}=\frac{13}{2}\).

Divide the standard deviation by \(\sqrt{5}\) to get estimated standard error \(\frac{\sqrt{130}}{10}\).

sections.title: Why use Student’s t instead of a normal reference?
sections.label: Choose t and its degrees of freedom
sections.intro: With a small random sample from a normal population and unknown variance, the denominator estimates variability from the same observations.

blocks.html: The statistic under \(H_0:\mu=\mu_0\) is \(T=\frac{\bar X-\mu_0}{\frac{S}{\sqrt n}}\) with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom.
A small sample size alone says nothing about the shape of the population.

blocks.title: Use the alternative to select the reference tail
blocks.prompt:
An independent random sample from a normal population with unknown variance gives \(n=10,\ \bar x=12,\ s^2=9\).

Use \(\mu\) for the population mean.

Test \(H_0:\mu=10\) against \(H_1:\mu\ne10\) at \(5\) per cent.

Give the statistic to 3 decimal places and the degrees of freedom.

retry.feedback: Keep the order of the comparison: subtract the null contrast from the observed contrast.

blocks.hint: Select the sampling design and standard error first. Choose the reference tail from the alternative, before using the sample result.
blocks.solution:
Use the two tails beyond the magnitude of the statistic specified by the alternative. The standard error calculation is \(\mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{9}{10}}=\frac{3 \sqrt{10}}{10}\).

Standardise the observed estimate after subtracting the null value. This gives \(t=\frac{2 \sqrt{10}}{3}\), or \(2.108\) to 3 decimal places. Use t with 9 degrees of freedom.

The p-value is \(0.0643\) to 4 decimal places. It lies above the significance level, so do not reject the null.

sections.title: How do I choose one or two tails?
sections.label: Read the alternative
sections.intro: Write hypotheses about the population mean before looking at the sample. The level \(\alpha\) sizes the fixed critical region. The p-value measures how far into the chosen tail the observed statistic falls.

blocks.html: Greater selects the upper tail, less selects the lower tail, and a change in either direction uses both tails.
A negative statistic does not turn a preselected upper-tail test into a lower-tail test.

AlternativeReference tail
\(\mu>\mu_0\)Upper
\(\mu<\mu_0\)Lower
\(\mu\ne\mu_0\)Both

blocks.title: Read the alternative hypothesis before the sample
blocks.prompt:
A laboratory wants to detect any change from the target population mean, whichever direction it takes.

Which alternative and reference tail match the study?
blocks.hint: The direction of the alternative comes from the question, not the sign of a later sample result.
blocks.solution: The population mean is the parameter. The study calls for \(H_1:\mu\ne\mu_0\), so use the two tails.

sections.title: What do I calculate for an upper-tail decision?
sections.label: Standardise and compare
sections.intro: Subtract the null mean from the observed mean, then divide by the estimated standard error.

blocks.html: For an upper-tail test at level \(\alpha\), find the column labelled \(1-\alpha\) in the Cambridge MF19 t-table. Its heading gives the area to the left of the cutoff. Use row \(\nu=n-1\). Reject \(H_0\) when the observed statistic lies beyond the cutoff on the right.

figure.alt: The ten-degrees-of-freedom t curve with the right-hand 5% critical region starting at 1.812.
figure.caption: Choose the cutoff before seeing the sample.

blocks.html: Do not use the sample standard deviation as the standard error of the mean.

blocks.title: Use the alternative to select the reference tail
blocks.prompt:
An independent random sample from a normal population with unknown variance gives \(n=9,\ \bar x=\frac{41}{5},\ s^2=9\).

Use \(\mu\) for the population mean.

Test \(H_0:\mu=7\) against \(H_1:\mu>7\) at \(5\) per cent.

Give the test statistic to 3 decimal places and select the decision.

retry.feedback: Keep the order of the comparison: subtract the null contrast from the observed contrast.

fields.label: Decision at the stated significance level

blocks.hint: Select the sampling design and standard error first. Choose the reference tail from the alternative, before using the sample result.
blocks.solution:
Use the upper tail specified by the alternative. The standard error calculation is \(\mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{9}{9}}=1\).

Standardise the observed estimate after subtracting the null value. This gives \(t=\frac{6}{5}\), or \(1.200\) to 3 decimal places. Use t with 8 degrees of freedom.

The p-value is \(0.1322\) to 4 decimal places. It lies above the significance level, so do not reject the null.

For this upper-tail check use MF19 row \(8\) and column \(0.950\): \(1.200<1.860\).

blocks.html: The observed tail starts at \(t_{\rm obs}\). Its area is the one-sided p-value. Compare it with the fixed critical region above.

figure.alt: The ten-degrees-of-freedom t curve with the observed upper tail starting at the statistic 1.990.
figure.caption: The observed statistic sets the p-value boundary.

sections.title: How does the decision change with a two-sided alternative?
sections.label: Use both extremes
sections.intro: With a symmetric t distribution, compare the distance from zero with the corresponding two-sided critical value.

blocks.html: For a two-sided alternative, double the one reference tail beyond the magnitude of the statistic.

figure.alt: Symmetric t curve with the two outside tails shaded beyond both critical cutoffs.
figure.caption: A two-sided test splits its significance level equally across the two tails.

blocks.html: Putting the entire significance level in one tail gives a different test.

blocks.title: Use the alternative to select the reference tail
blocks.prompt:
An independent random sample from a normal population with unknown variance gives \(n=16,\ \bar x=\frac{35}{2},\ s^2=4\).

Use \(\mu\) for the population mean.

Test \(H_0:\mu=19\) against \(H_1:\mu\ne19\) at \(5\) per cent.

retry.feedback: Keep the order of the comparison: subtract the null contrast from the observed contrast.

fields.label: Decision at the stated significance level

blocks.hint: Select the sampling design and standard error first. Choose the reference tail from the alternative, before using the sample result.
blocks.solution:
Use the two tails beyond the magnitude of the statistic specified by the alternative. The standard error calculation is \(\mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{4}{16}}=\frac{1}{2}\).

Standardise the observed estimate after subtracting the null value. This gives \(t=-3\), or \(-3.000\) to 3 decimal places. Use t with 15 degrees of freedom.

The p-value is \(0.0090\) to 4 decimal places. It lies below the significance level, so reject the null.

Use row \(15\), column \(0.975\): \(|t_{\rm obs}|=3.000>2.131\).

sections.title: What does a non-significant result mean?
sections.label: State the evidence carefully
sections.intro: A sample may provide insufficient evidence against the null. That is a conclusion about this test at its specified level.

blocks.html: Write the decision, significance level and the context of the alternative. Lack of evidence does not establish an exact population mean.
Avoid treating the p-value as the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

blocks.hint: Select the sampling design and standard error first. Choose the reference tail from the alternative, before using the sample result.

examples.title: Recover the sample mean, variance and estimated standard error
examples.question:
The observations are \(3,\quad 6,\quad 7,\quad 8,\quad 11\).

Find the original mean, unbiased sample variance and estimated standard error of the mean. Give exact values.
solution: The sum is \(35\) and the sum of squares is \(279\). The sample has \(5\) observations.
After undoing any coding, the mean is \(7\). The unbiased variance is \(\frac{279-\frac{\left(35\right)^2}{5}}{4}=\frac{17}{2}\).
Divide the standard deviation by \(\sqrt{5}\) to get estimated standard error \(\frac{\sqrt{170}}{10}\).

examples.title: Recover the sample mean, variance and estimated standard error
examples.question:
The coded observations \(y=x-30\) are \(-7,\quad -2,\quad 1,\quad 1,\quad 2\).

Find the original mean, unbiased sample variance and estimated standard error of the mean. Give exact values.
solution: The sum is \(-5\) and the sum of squares is \(59\). The sample has \(5\) observations.
After undoing any coding, the mean is \(29\). The unbiased variance is \(\frac{59-\frac{\left(-5\right)^2}{5}}{4}=\frac{27}{2}\).
Divide the standard deviation by \(\sqrt{5}\) to get estimated standard error \(\frac{3 \sqrt{30}}{10}\).

examples.title: Identify the model from the sampling design
examples.question:
A random sample of twelve readings comes from one normal population with unknown variance.

Which procedure matches this design?
solution: There is a single sample from a normal population and its variance is unknown.
Standardise the sample mean using \(\frac{s}{\sqrt{12}}\). Under the null hypothesis this gives a one-sample \(t\) statistic with \(11\) degrees of freedom.

examples.title: Read the alternative hypothesis before the sample
examples.question:
A manufacturer tests whether a modification reduced the population mean processing time below its baseline.

Which alternative and reference tail match the study?
solution: The population mean is the parameter. The study calls for \(H_1:\mu<\mu_0\), so use the lower tail.
Set \(H_0:\mu=\mu_0\). A sample giving a sufficiently negative test statistic supports a decrease, so use the lower-tail probability under \(H_0\).

examples.title: Test whether the mean bottle fill has risen
examples.question: Assume independent fill volumes from a normal population with unknown variance. A random sample gives \(n=11\), \(\bar x=5.2\,\mathrm{mL}\), \(s^2=4\,\mathrm{mL}^2\). At the \(5\%\) level, test whether the population mean exceeds \(4\,\mathrm{mL}\).
solution: Let \(\mu\) be the population mean fill volume. Write \(H_0:\mu=4\) and \(H_1:\mu>4\) before computing anything. Normality and unknown variance give a one-sample \(t\)-test with \(\nu=11-1=10\).
The estimated standard error is \(\frac{2}{\sqrt{11}}\,\mathrm{mL}\). Thus \(t_{\rm obs}=\frac{5.2-4}{2/\sqrt{11}}\approx1.990\).
Use MF19 row \(10\), column \(0.950\). The critical value is \(1.812\). Since \(1.990>1.812\), reject \(H_0\). At the \(5\%\) level there is evidence that the mean fill exceeds \(4\,\mathrm{mL}\).

For an optional numerical p-value, use a Student \(t\) cumulative distribution function with \(\nu=10\). Subtract its value at the unrounded statistic from one, for example scipy.stats.t.sf(1.2*sqrt(11)/2, 10) with sqrt from math. This gives \(p\approx0.0373\). The MF19 row can bracket the p-value between \(0.025\) and \(0.050\) using cutoffs \(2.228\) and \(1.812\).

examples.title: Check for a change in mean drying time
examples.question: Assume independent drying times from a normal population with unknown variance. A random sample gives \(n=8\), \(\bar x=18\) minutes and \(s^2=16\) square minutes. At the \(5\%\) level, test whether the population mean differs from \(21\) minutes.
solution: Write \(H_0:\mu=21\) and \(H_1:\mu\ne21\), where \(\mu\) is the population mean drying time in minutes. Both tails count, and \(\nu=7\).
Use \(s=4\) and compute \(t_{\rm obs}=\frac{18-21}{4/\sqrt8}\approx-2.121\). The statistic points to the left, so compare its distance from zero with the positive cutoff.

Each tail has area \(0.025\). From MF19 row \(7\), column \(0.975\), the boundaries are \(-2.365\) and \(2.365\). Since \(|t_{\rm obs}|=2.121<2.365\), do not reject \(H_0\). At the \(5\%\) level there is insufficient evidence that the mean differs from \(21\) minutes.

With a Student \(t\) function, the two-sided p-value is twice the upper-tail probability beyond \(|t_{\rm obs}|\), for example 2*scipy.stats.t.sf(3*sqrt(8)/4, 7). The critical-value route above completes the test using MF19.

examples.title: Report insufficient evidence for a lower mean
examples.question: At a drying station, an independent random sample from a normal population with unknown variance gives \(n=10\), \(\bar x=8.3\) minutes and \(s^2=16\) square minutes. Test whether the mean is below \(9\) minutes at the \(5\%\) level.
solution: Set \(H_0:\mu=9\), \(H_1:\mu<9\) and \(\nu=9\). The statistic is \(t_{\rm obs}=\frac{8.3-9}{4/\sqrt{10}}\approx-0.553\).
Read \(1.833\) from row \(9\), column \(0.950\). By symmetry the lower-tail cutoff is \(-1.833\), so \(-0.553\) lies outside the rejection region.
Do not reject \(H_0\). At the \(5\%\) level the sample gives insufficient evidence that the mean drying time is below \(9\) minutes. The data leave the original mean possible.

stats_inference_normal.description: Compare independent population means with known variances or a large-sample normal approximation, and interpret the selected tail.

sections.title: Why do the variance terms add even when means are subtracted?
sections.label: Add independent contributions
sections.intro: Successive samples give two random means. The variance of their difference includes the variability of both when they are independent.

blocks.html: For independent samples use \(\frac{\sigma_A^2}{n_A}+\frac{\sigma_B^2}{n_B}\) for the variance of the difference.
A minus sign in the estimate changes its order. It does not make a variance term negative.

blocks.title: Use the alternative to select the reference tail
blocks.prompt:
Independent random samples come from two normal populations with known variances. The summaries are \(n_A=9,\ \bar a=15,\ \sigma_A^2=9\) and \(n_B=16,\ \bar b=14,\ \sigma_B^2=16\).

Use \(\mu_A-\mu_B\) for the population mean difference.

Test \(H_0:\mu_A-\mu_B=0\) against \(H_1:\mu_A-\mu_B\ne0\) at \(5\) per cent.

Give the statistic to 3 decimal places.

retry.feedback: Keep the order of the comparison: subtract the null contrast from the observed contrast.

blocks.hint: Select the sampling design and standard error first. Choose the reference tail from the alternative, before using the sample result.
blocks.solution:
Use the two tails beyond the magnitude of the statistic specified by the alternative. The standard error calculation is \(\mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{9}{9}+\frac{16}{16}}=\sqrt{2}\).

Standardise the observed estimate after subtracting the null value. This gives \(z=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\), or \(0.707\) to 3 decimal places. Use z from the standard normal.

The p-value is \(0.4795\) to 4 decimal places. It lies above the significance level, so do not reject the null.

sections.title: When is this normal calculation exact?
sections.label: Use the stated population variances
sections.intro: If the populations are normal and the variances are known, the standardised difference is exactly normal.

blocks.html: Use the stated population values rather than replacing them with hypothetical sample estimates.
Check whether the problem supplies a variance or a standard deviation.

sections.title: What if neither variance is known?
sections.label: Use separate large-sample estimates
sections.intro: For sufficiently large independent samples with finite variances, the separate sample variance estimates can be used in a normal approximation.

blocks.html: The large-sample standard error uses each sample variance with its own sample size. Do not assume the two population variances agree.
A large sample does not repair biased selection or dependence.

blocks.title: Use the alternative to select the reference tail
blocks.prompt:
Two independent large random samples are taken from different populations of finite variance. The summaries are \(n_A=64,\ \bar a=\frac{277}{10},\ s_A^2=25\) and \(n_B=100,\ \bar b=26,\ s_B^2=36\).

Use \(\mu_A-\mu_B\) for the population mean difference.

Give the test statistic to 3 decimal places and select the decision.

sections.title: Can the null difference be non-zero?
sections.label: Centre on the claimed contrast
sections.intro: A question may ask whether one mean is a stated amount greater than the other. Define the first minus the second and subtract that null amount.

blocks.html: The test numerator is \((\bar a-\bar b)-\delta_0\). Keep the same contrast throughout.

sections.title: Does an independent normal method fit every comparison?
sections.label: Distinguish the sampling designs
sections.intro: Before choosing a procedure, identify whether values are independent or paired and whether the variances are known.

blocks.html: Small independent normal samples can use a pooled t method if the same unknown variance is assumed. Matched measurements instead use differences.
Similarity of two observed variances is not by itself a common population variance assumption.

blocks.title: Identify the model from the sampling design
blocks.prompt:
Two large independent random samples of finite variance have unequal and unknown population variances.

Which procedure matches this design?
blocks.hint: Identify the sample units, then check the variance and normality information.
blocks.solution: Independent samples have known normal variances or are sufficiently large for the normal approximation, as stated.

examples.title: Use the alternative to select the reference tail
examples.question:
Independent random samples come from two normal populations with known variances. The summaries are \(n_A=16,\ \bar a=24,\ \sigma_A^2=4\) and \(n_B=25,\ \bar b=23,\ \sigma_B^2=9\).

Use \(\mu_A-\mu_B\) for the population mean difference.

Test \(H_0:\mu_A-\mu_B=0\) against \(H_1:\mu_A-\mu_B\ne0\) at \(5\) per cent.

Give the statistic to 3 decimal places.
solution: Use the two tails beyond the magnitude of the statistic specified by the alternative. The standard error calculation is \(\mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{4}{16}+\frac{9}{25}}=\frac{\sqrt{61}}{10}\).
Standardise the observed estimate after subtracting the null value. This gives \(z=\frac{10 \sqrt{61}}{61}\), or \(1.280\) to 3 decimal places. Use z from the standard normal.
The p-value is \(0.2004\) to 4 decimal places. It lies above the significance level, so do not reject the null.

examples.title: Identify the model from the sampling design
examples.question:
Two independent samples of sizes 16 and 25 come from normal populations with known variances.

Which procedure matches this design?
solution: Independent samples have known normal variances or are sufficiently large for the normal approximation, as stated.
Use the two-sample normal test. Independence gives the variance of the difference as \(\frac{\sigma_1^2}{16}+\frac{\sigma_2^2}{25}\), using the two known population variances.

blocks.html: A pooled estimate concerns one shared scale. It is not a universal alternative for any pair of samples.

sections.title: Why is the pooled estimate weighted?
sections.label: Combine centred squares
sections.intro: Each sample variance is its own centred sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom.

blocks.html: Recover the two numerators and divide their sum by \(n_A+n_B-2\).
A simple average gives the right weights only when sample sizes agree or the two variances happen to be identical.

SampleCentred sum of squares
A\((n_A-1)s_A^2\)
B\((n_B-1)s_B^2\)

blocks.title: Recover a variance using the two degrees-of-freedom weights
blocks.prompt:
Independent random samples come from two normal populations with a common unknown variance. The summaries are \(n_A=6,\ \bar a=12,\ s_A^2=4\) and \(n_B=10,\ \bar b=11,\ s_B^2=8\).

Find the pooled variance exactly and state the reference degrees of freedom.
blocks.hint: Weight each variance by its sample's degrees of freedom.
blocks.solution:
A contributes \(20\) to the centred sum of squares. The combined degrees of freedom are \(14\).

Divide the combined centred sum \(92\) by \(14\) to obtain \(\frac{46}{7}\).

sections.title: How can I pool when only raw scores are given?

blocks.html: Centre within each group and then add the centred sums. Centring all observations around a single grand mean answers a different question.
Do not discard the sample labels before calculating variability.

blocks.title: Recover a variance using the two degrees-of-freedom weights
blocks.prompt:
Two small independent random samples are from normal populations with a common unknown variance.

Sample A gives \(12,\quad 13,\quad 13,\quad 16,\quad 16\). Sample B gives \(10,\quad 11,\quad 13,\quad 14\).

Find the pooled variance and its degrees of freedom.
blocks.hint: Weight each variance by its sample's degrees of freedom.
blocks.solution:
After centring separately, the unbiased variances are \(\frac{7}{2}\) and \(\frac{10}{3}\).

A contributes \(14\) to the centred sum of squares. The combined degrees of freedom are \(7\).

Divide the combined centred sum \(24\) by \(7\) to obtain \(\frac{24}{7}\).

sections.title: Which standard error belongs to the pooled statistic?

blocks.html: \(\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}=s_p\sqrt{\frac1{n_A}+\frac1{n_B}}\). Use a t reference under the null.
Use the square root of the pooled variance. The variance itself has squared measurement units.

Independent random samples come from two normal populations with a common unknown variance. The summaries are \(n_A=11,\ \bar a=21,\ s_A^2=4\) and \(n_B=15,\ \bar b=19,\ s_B^2=9\).

Use \(\mu_A-\mu_B\) for the population mean difference.

Test \(H_0:\mu_A-\mu_B=0\) against \(H_1:\mu_A-\mu_B\ne0\) at \(5\) per cent.

Give the statistic to 3 decimal places and the degrees of freedom.

retry.feedback: Keep the order of the comparison: subtract the null contrast from the observed contrast.

extraPractice.hint: Select the sampling design and standard error first. Choose the reference tail from the alternative, before using the sample result.
extraPractice.solution:
Use the two tails beyond the magnitude of the statistic specified by the alternative. The standard error calculation is \(s_p^2=\frac{83}{12},\quad \mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{83}{12}\left(\frac{1}{11}+\frac{1}{15}\right)}=\frac{\sqrt{118690}}{330}\).

Standardise the observed estimate after subtracting the null value. This gives \(t=\frac{6 \sqrt{118690}}{1079}\), or \(1.916\) to 3 decimal places. Use t with 24 degrees of freedom.

The p-value is \(0.0674\) to 4 decimal places. It lies above the significance level, so do not reject the null.

stats_inference_intervals.description: Construct and interpret confidence intervals for a normal mean with unknown variance, including reverse calculations from known endpoints.

sections.title: What goes on either side of the estimate?
sections.label: Use estimate plus or minus a margin
sections.intro: A central confidence interval consists of a point estimate plus or minus a critical multiplier times the estimated standard error.

blocks.html: For a normal mean with unknown variance, use \(\bar x\pm t_{n-1,\,1-\frac{\alpha}{2}}\frac{s}{\sqrt n}\).

figure.alt: Closed horizontal confidence interval with labelled lower endpoint, centre and upper endpoint. Equal spans from the centre to each side.
figure.caption: The margin is the distance from the estimate to either endpoint.

blocks.html: Keep both endpoints. The margin is half the distance between them.

blocks.title: Construct an interval in the requested order
blocks.prompt:
An independent random sample from a normal population with unknown variance gives \(n=12,\ \bar x=37,\ s^2=\frac{25}{4}\).

Find a \(95\) per cent confidence interval for \(\mu\). Use the supplied critical value \(2.201\) exactly. Give endpoints to 3 decimal places.
blocks.hint: Use estimate plus or minus a two-sided margin. If reversing a difference, the former upper endpoint gives the new lower endpoint.
blocks.solution:
The calculated standard error comes from \(\mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{\frac{25}{4}}{12}}=\frac{5 \sqrt{3}}{12}\).

The margin is \(\frac{2201}{1000}\times\frac{5 \sqrt{3}}{12}\). Centre the interval at the observed estimate.

The requested endpoints are \(35.412\) and \(38.588\).

sections.intro: For a central interval, the two outer reference tails carry equal probability. Use that tail area and the appropriate degrees of freedom.

blocks.html: When a critical value is supplied, use it as instructed. Keep all other calculations unrounded until the final endpoints.

sections.label: Build the standard error
sections.intro: Fix the order first. For independent normal samples with known variances, the contrast uses a normal reference.

Independent random samples come from two normal populations with a common unknown variance. The summaries are \(n_A=7,\ \bar a=17,\ s_A^2=3\) and \(n_B=9,\ \bar b=16,\ s_B^2=5\).

Find a \(95\) per cent confidence interval for \(\mu_A-\mu_B\). Use the supplied critical value \(2.145\) exactly. Give endpoints to 3 decimal places.
extraPractice.hint: Use estimate plus or minus a two-sided margin. If reversing a difference, the former upper endpoint gives the new lower endpoint.
extraPractice.solution:
The calculated standard error comes from \(s_p^2=\frac{29}{7},\quad \mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{29}{7}\left(\frac{1}{7}+\frac{1}{9}\right)}=\frac{4 \sqrt{29}}{21}\).

The margin is \(\frac{429}{200}\times\frac{4 \sqrt{29}}{21}\). Centre the interval at the observed estimate.

The requested endpoints are \(-1.200\) and \(3.200\).

extraPractice.title: Construct an interval in the requested order
extraPractice.prompt:
Use the following independent before-and-after pairs. Assume the differences before minus after follow a normal model.

PairBeforeAfter
1\(17\)\(16\)
2\(19\)\(18\)
3\(22\)\(22\)
4\(21\)\(20\)
5\(23\)\(21\)

Find a \(95\) per cent confidence interval for \(\mu_d\). Use the supplied critical value \(2.776\) exactly. Give endpoints to 3 decimal places.
extraPractice.hint: Use estimate plus or minus a two-sided margin. If reversing a difference, the former upper endpoint gives the new lower endpoint.
extraPractice.solution:
Subtract second from first within each pair to obtain \(1,\quad 1,\quad 0,\quad 1,\quad 2\).

The mean difference is \(1\). The unbiased variance of these differences is \(\frac{1}{2}\).

The calculated standard error comes from \(\mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{5}}=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}\).

The margin is \(\frac{347}{125}\times\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}\). Centre the interval at the observed estimate.

The requested endpoints are \(0.122\) and \(1.878\).

extraPractice.title: Construct an interval in the requested order
extraPractice.prompt:
Independent random samples come from two normal populations with a common unknown variance. The summaries are \(n_A=12,\ \bar a=19,\ s_A^2=9\) and \(n_B=10,\ \bar b=16,\ s_B^2=4\).

Find a \(95\) per cent confidence interval for \(\mu_B-\mu_A\). Use the supplied critical value \(2.086\) exactly. Give endpoints to 3 decimal places.
extraPractice.hint: Use estimate plus or minus a two-sided margin. If reversing a difference, the former upper endpoint gives the new lower endpoint.
extraPractice.solution:
The calculated standard error comes from \(s_p^2=\frac{27}{4},\quad \mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{27}{4}\left(\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{10}\right)}=\frac{3 \sqrt{55}}{20}\).

The margin is \(\frac{1043}{500}\times\frac{3 \sqrt{55}}{20}\). Negate the estimate to put the difference in the requested order.

The requested endpoints are \(-5.321\) and \(-0.679\).

extraPractice.title: Read whether a proposed value lies inside the interval
extraPractice.prompt: A confidence procedure for a mean produces interval \([-3,-1]\). Consider the corresponding two-sided test at the matching significance level for null value \(0\). Is the value inside the interval?
extraPractice.hint: Use the interval and the matching two-sided test at the specified level.
extraPractice.solution:
Compare \(0\) with both endpoints \(-3\) and \(-1\).

The value is outside, so the corresponding two-sided test would reject.
